table.title: Object recognition in ASD: Shape configuration and Category-specificity
table.research_questions:
•	Hypothesis 1 (H1): Individuals with ASD will show reduced performance with recognition of fragmented objects relative to neurotypicals on a difficult object decision task.

•	H2: Individuals with ASD will show performance within the normal range on recognition of silhouetted objects compared with neurotypicals on a difficult object decision task.

•	H3: If H1 is supported we expect autistic individuals with reduced performance relative to neurotypicals on the object recognition task with fragmented stimuli (z < -1.5) to obtain a lower score on a Local-Global composite index derived from Navon’s paradigm (Gerlach & Poirel, 2020) compared with ASD individuals who are not impaired with recognition of fragmented forms on the object recognition task (z > - 1.5).

•	H4: Individuals with ASD will show more impaired processing of natural objects compared with artefacts relative to neurotypical individuals and this difference will be more pronounced with fragmented stimuli than with regular line-drawings.

•	H5: Individuals with ASD will show reduced performance relative to neurotypicals for natural objects also in object classification tasks that do not require object individuation (superordinate classification). Autistic individuals’ superordinate classification performance for artefacts will, however, fall within the range of neurotypicals.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
The participants took part in a series of surveys/experiments conducted over 2-3 sessions. 

This study will examine the results from five of these experiments:

•	A difficult object decision task with regular line-drawings as described in Gerlach and Toft (2011).

•	A difficult object decision task with fragmented stimuli as described in Gerlach and Toft (2011).

•	A difficult object decision task with silhouettes as described in Gerlach and Toft (2011).

•	A superordinate object classification task as described in Gerlach and Marques (2014).

•	Navon’s paradigm as described in Gerlach and Poirel (2020).

All participants performed the experiments in the order as given above.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to accessing the data
table.existing_data_explanation:
We have collected data from 41 individuals with ASD and 41 age, education, gender and IQ matched neurotypical individuals.
 
Eligibility criteria for all participants (both ASD and control) included: being between 18 and 70 years of age, fluency in Danish, having normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and an IQ score above 70. 
All participants who had an ADD or ADHD diagnosis, or had a neurological disorder, such as epilepsy, apoplexy, Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, or severe head trauma were excluded. 

ASD-participants were required to have a formal diagnosis of ASD based on psychiatric or psychological evaluation. To further quantify the ASD characteristics of the participants, ADOS scores was collected for all ASD participants, either by new testing or by requesting access to existing data. Further, both ASD and control participants completed the Autism Quotient (AQ) questionnaire (Baron-Cohen, Wheelwright, Skinner, Martin, & Clubley, 2001) and the Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS-2)(Constantino & Gruber, 2012). Control participants with a lifetime history of an ASD diagnosis or a scoring of 32 or higher on the AQ were excluded from the study. 

The data were acquired and stored by personnel how did not partake in the formulation of the hypotheses, and the researchers who did formulate them will not access/process the data prior to the registration. Access to the data is limited and logged.
table.data_collection_procedures:
Participants with ASD were recruited by announcement in Facebook groups with a relevant reach to autistic adults, through posters at the campus of University of Southern Denmark (SDU), and presentations at network meetings within autistic communities in Denmark. 

Control participants were recruited through posters at the SDU Odense Campus and in larger Facebook groups (such as “Medical Students at University of Southern Denmark”). To match the control group to the ASD group on estimated IQ a purposeful recruitment was also made through announcement of the project in a Facebook group for members of Mensa Denmark.
table.sample_size: We aimed for the inclusion of 40 participants with ASD and 40 matched neurotypical control participants.
table.sample_size_rationale: This sample size is twice that reported in the reference studies that examining object recognition performance in ASD (Burnett et al., 2015; Evers et al., 2014). The limit of 40 participants with ASD and 40 matched neurotypical control participants was set for practical reasons as this figure was deemed feasible to reach in the period for which we had obtained funding to conduct the study (2 years).
table.measured_variables:
•	The dependent variables in the three object decision tasks will be reaction time (RT) and accuracy. As in previous studies using these tasks, the analyses will be based on responses to real objects only (Gerlach & Marques, 2014; Gerlach & Toft, 2011). RT (median correct) and accuracy will be combined into a single dependent measure by means of the Balanced Integration Score (BIS) (Liesefeld, Fu, & Zimmer, 2015; Liesefeld & Janczyk, 2019).

•	The dependent variables in the superordinate object classification task will be RT and accuracy combined into a single dependent measure (the BIS).

•	Navon’s paradigm as setup by Gerlach and Poirel (2020). The dependent variable will be RT (correct trials only) as error rates are typically low in this setup.
table.indices: •	Navon’s paradigm: The Global-Local composite index will be based on the difference in RT to local and global identity judgements on inconsistent trials only. The index will be computed for each participant as a standardized mean difference (Cohen's d), that is, as the difference between the two means of interest divided by their pooled standard deviations. Prior to computing the index, the data for correct trials will be trimmed for each participant excluding any RT that falls above or below 2½ SDs from the mean of a given participant for each of the four main conditions comprising the Navon paradigm (global consistent, global inconsistent, local consistent & local inconsistent).
table.statistical_tests:
The statistical analyses for testing each hypothesis are listed below.  
•	H1: Group differences will be examined with unpaired t-tests based on bias corrected and accelerated bootstrap analyses [1000 samples].

•	H2: Independent samples t-test based on Bayesian inference.

•	H3: Group differences will be examined with unpaired t-tests based on bias corrected and accelerated bootstrap analyses [1000 samples].

•	H4: Interactions and main effects will be examined by means of a mixed factorial ANOVA with Group (Individuals with ASD vs neurotypicals), as a between-subject factor and StimulusType (regular drawings vs fragmented drawings) and Category (natural objects vs artefacts) as within-subject factors. Interactions will be examined by contrasts among the marginal means (t-tests based on bias corrected and accelerated bootstrap analyses [1000 samples]).

•	H5: Interactions and main effects will be examined by means of a mixed factorial ANOVA with Group (Individuals with ASD vs neurotypicals), as a between-subject factor and Category (natural objects vs artefacts) as within-subject factors. Interactions will be examined by contrasts (t-tests) among the marginal means based on Bayesian inference.
table.inference_criteria:
•	H1: Because the prediction is directional, the effect will be considered significant if the lower bound of the (two-tailed) bootstrapped 90% CI of the statistical tests is not positive (BIS will be higher for neurotypicals than individuals with ASD). Effect sizes will be indexed by Cohen’s d.

•	H2: The effect will be assessed by means of the associated Bayes factors based on Zellner-Siow’s approach.

•	H3: Because the prediction is directional, the effect will be considered significant if the lower bound of the (two-tailed) bootstrapped 90% CI of the statistical tests is not negative (scores on the Global-Local composite index will be higher for neurotypicals than individuals with ASD). Effect sizes will be indexed by Cohen’s d.

•	H4: Because the predictions are directional, effects in the ANOVA will be considered significant if the one-tailed p-value is < .05. For planned post-hoc comparisons (among the marginal means) effects will be considered significant if the lower bound of the (two-tailed) bootstrapped 90% CI of the statistical tests is not negative (BIS will be higher for: neurotypicals than individuals with ASD, higher for line-drawings than for fragmented forms, and higher for natural objects than for artefacts). Effect sizes for the ANOVA will be indexed by partial eta squared and for the planned post-hoc comparisons as Cohen’s d.

•	H5: Because the prediction is directional, effects in the ANOVA will be considered significant if the one-tailed p-value for the interaction is < .05. For planned post-hoc comparisons (among the marginal means): the effect for natural objects will be considered significant if the lower bound of the (two-tailed) 90% credible interval of the statistical tests for the contrast between individuals with ASD and neurotypicals is not negative (BIS scores will be higher for neurotypicals than for individuals with ASD): the effect for artefacts is not expected to be credible for which reason the 95% credible interval is expected to cover both positive and negative values.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Data from participants who did not complete all included measures for the relevant comparisons will be excluded from the data set.
table.missing_data_handling: Data from participants who did not complete all included measures for the relevant comparisons will be excluded from the data set.

text.text: Face recognition in autism is well-researched and up to 1/3 of autistic individuals are reported to have severe face recognition difficulties.
In comparison, there are few reports on object recognition performance in autism, and the findings are rather inconsistent.
Here we report results from a series of object recognition tasks performed by autistic (N = 41) and matched non-autistic participants.

Across tasks we varied the demand placed on perceptual differentiation, the structural similarity of the objects, and the salience and value of global shape information (the object's bounding contour) relative to local shape information (details) in the recognition process.

Our main hypothesis was that when local shape information was less salient than global shape information, and when both types of information needed to be integrated to support performance, autistic participants would perform less efficiently than non-autistic participants.
This hypothesis was not fulfilled as the autistic group performed just as efficiently as the non-autistic group across all tasks.

We discuss our findings in the context of previous reports of object recognition performance in autism and argue that former reports of impairments might reflect lexico-semantic rather than perceptual processes.

text.text: PACE assumes the existence of two stages in visual object recognition: shape configuration and selection, which are held to be differentially affected by the structural similarity among objects and their visual complexity (Gerlach & Marques, 2014).

text.text: Shape configuration is the binding of visual elements into elaborate shape descriptions corresponding to whole objects or large object parts in which relationships between the parts are specified.
Shape configuration should thus be distinguished from low-level grouping processes such as grouping by proximity, collinearity (alignment), color, etc.

While these grouping operations do integrate elements in the visual scene, they require little shape configuration besides the ability to determine for example the orientation of the elements (Gerlach, 2009).
text.formatted: While these grouping operations do integrate elements in the visual scene, they require little shape configuration besides the ability to determine for example the orientation of the elements <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gerlach, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The configured shape representation is a description that -at the stage of selection -is matched with structural representations of whole objects or large object parts stored in visual long-term memory (VLTM).
The process of finding a match between the configured representation and VLTM representations is considered as a race among VLTM representations that compete for selection.
The VLTM representation that best matches the configured representation will be selected.
The match criterion is flexible and also task dependent.
If the task requires fine-grained discrimination, as in subordinate classification (e.g., "Is this a bulldog or a bull terrier?"), an elaborate match criterion will be in place.
If the task only requires gross perceptual processing, as in superordinate classification (e.g., "Is this a natural object or an artefact?"), a more liberal match criterion will suffice.
When the configured representation is matched with VLTM representations according to a given criterion, the object is recognized at a structural (but not yet a semantic) level.

An important assumption in PACE is that shape configuration follows a first pass access to VLTM representations based on global object contour -the object's outer bounding line -which yields initial hypotheses concerning the likely identity of the stimulus (Gerlach & Toft, 2011).
text.formatted: An important assumption in PACE is that shape configuration follows a first pass access to VLTM representations based on global object contour -the object's outer bounding line -which yields initial hypotheses concerning the likely identity of the stimulus <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Gerlach & Toft, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: These hypotheses are then used in a top-down manner to augment the build-up of a more detailed description of the stimulus (i.e., shape configuration) which again serves as input for a more specific match with VLTM representations (the selection stage).

Hence, object recognition may take place without shape configuration, based mainly then on the object's bounding contour or perceptually unconnected details, but the identification process is then likely to be (abnormally) slow and error prone.

This type of behavior is seen in integrative agnosia where patients seem to piece together a useful description of the stimulus bit by bit (Behrmann & Kimchi, 2003; Behrmann & Williams, 2007; Gerlach et al., 2005).

text.text: Shape configuration is thus an important part of normal visual object processing which operates recurrently until a successful match between the stimulus and VLTM representations has been obtained (following a coarse-to-fine temporal dynamic) (Gerlach, 2017b; Sanocki, 1993; Schyns & Oliva, 1994).

text.text: In PACE, fast derivation of global shape information is deemed significant in the recognition process because it: (i) facilitates the matching process proper by narrowing down the scope of likely VLTM candidates (via the "quick and dirty" first pass activation of VLTM representations), and (ii) provides the initial frame in which local details can later be embedded (the process of shape configuration).
Importantly there is evidence suggesting that these aspects of global shape processing are likely to reflect independent mechanisms (Gerlach & Poirel, 2018).
text.formatted: Importantly there is evidence suggesting that these aspects of global shape processing are likely to reflect independent mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Gerlach & Poirel, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A final aspect to be considered is how shape configuration and selection are differentially affected by the structural similarity of the objects to be recognized.

According to PACE, objects belonging to categories with high structural similarity (SS objects) will activate a greater range of structurally related VLTM representations compared with objects belonging to categories which are more structurally distinct (SD objects).

The consequence of the greater competition for SS objects is that the matching process (selection stage) for these objects will be slower and more error prone than the matching process for SD objects.
In comparison, at the stage of shape configuration SS objects enjoy an advantage.

This assumption is based on the following premises: (i) global shape characteristics may be processed earlier on in time than local shape characteristics, providing the initial frame in which local details can later be embedded; (ii) global shape characteristics are more diagnostic of basic level object identity for SS than for SD objects; and (iii) information regarding object identity may augment shape configuration in a top-down manner (for discussion of evidence supporting these premises see Gerlach (2017b)).
text.formatted: This assumption is based on the following premises: (i) global shape characteristics may be processed earlier on in time than local shape characteristics, providing the initial frame in which local details can later be embedded; (ii) global shape characteristics are more diagnostic of basic level object identity for SS than for SD objects; and (iii) information regarding object identity may augment shape configuration in a top-down manner (for discussion of evidence supporting these premises see <ref type="bibr">Gerlach (2017b)</ref>).

text.text: As discussed above, autistic individuals: (i) (can) use global shape information when it is most salient, but (ii) seem to have difficulties when global and local information needs to be integrated (Happé & Frith, 2006; Mottron et al., 2006; Van Eylen et al., 2018).
text.formatted: As discussed above, autistic individuals: (i) (can) use global shape information when it is most salient, but (ii) seem to have difficulties when global and local information needs to be integrated <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Happé & Frith, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Mottron et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Van Eylen et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In PACE this can be interpreted as a normal first pass access to activation of VLTM representations (a process that is dominated by global shape information as this is the first type of information available), but difficulties with shape configuration because local details are weighted more than global shape when both types of information are available and need to be integrated.

Based on the PACE framework -and the assumption that autistic individuals have a local shape processing bias -we expected the following outcomes across a range of tasks where we manipulated the degree of structural similarity, stimulus characteristics (salience of global/local information), and task demands (degree of perceptual differentiation required): Autistic individuals will show reduced performance with recognition of fragmented objects relative to non-autistic individuals on a difficult object decision task (deciding whether stimuli depict real objects or nonobjects) (Hypothesis 1: H1).

This prediction follows from the assumptions that: (i) a difficult task with fragmented objects places particularly high demands on perceptual differentiation, and thus also shape configuration, and (ii) the use of global shape information will support the configuration process.
Hence, a local processing bias should thus be disadvantageous in this task.
In comparison, autistic individuals will show performance within the non-autistic range on recognition of silhouettes in a difficult object decision task (H2).

This prediction follows from the assumptions that: (i) global shape processing per se is not affected in autism, (ii) global shape is more salient than details Object recognition in autism 9 in silhouettes (Wagemans et al., 2008), and (iii) silhouette recognition does not rely on shape configuration (Gerlach et al., 2005; Riddoch & Humphreys, 1987).

text.text: Accordingly, a local shape bias should not impact much on task performance with silhouettes.

Regarding effects of structural similarity, autistic individuals will show reduced performance for SS objects compared with SD objects relative to non-autistic individuals and this difference will be more pronounced with fragmented stimuli than with regular drawings (H3).

In addition to the assumptions above, this supposition is based on the additional assumption that similarity in global shape is typically helpful in the shape configuration process (Gerlach & Toft, 2011).

text.text: Finally, autistic participants will show reduced performance relative to nonautistic participants for SS objects but not for SD objects in a superordinate classification task (H4).

This prediction is based on the assumption that global shape characteristics are typically processed faster than local shape characteristics, but that performance in the superordinate classification task can be based on both local and global information.
A local processing bias should thus be disadvantageous in this task.

text.text: In the present experiments we used category (natural objects vs artefacts) as a proxy for structural similarity.
Natural objects typically belong to categories characterized by high structural similarity and artefacts to categories with low(er) structural similarity.
Structural similarity has been operationalized differently by different authors.

Hence two different measures of structural similarity were used to assess this aspect of the present stimuli: (i) The degree of contour overlap (CO) among objects (Humphreys et al., 1988), and (ii) the degree of within-item structural diversity (WSD) among objects (Turnbull & Laws, 2000).

text.text: The measure of CO was generated by: (i) Normalizing all the pictures of objects in the Snodgrass and Vanderwart (1980) corpus for orientation and size, (ii) overlaying each picture on a grid with pictures of every other object from the same category (the categories being animals, birds, body parts, buildings, clothes, crustacea, fruit, furniture, implements, insects, vegetables, and vehicles), and (iii) calculating the average overlap between the pictures on their bounding contour -that is, on their outline shape without consideration of internal details -as a function of the amount of contour in each target picture.

text.text: The measure of WSD, which is also based on the Snodgrass and Vanderwart corpus, was derived by presenting individuals with the name of an object and asking them to rate the extent to which instances with that name had similar structural representations (on a scale from 1-5;1 = very dissimilar;5 = very similar).

The WSD measure can be considered a high-level measure of structural similarity because it is based on memories of objects rather than on the physical properties of objects (drawings) such as the CO measure (Gerlach, 2017a).

text.text: All stimuli were presented centrally on a white background on a PC monitor and subtended 3-5° of visual angle.
The stimuli were displayed until subjects made a response.
The interval between response and presentation of the next object was 1 s.
RTs were recorded using a serial response box.
Participants were encouraged to respond as fast and as accurately as possible.
Prior to each of the tasks the participants performed a practice version of the upcoming task.
The stimuli used in these practice tasks were not used in the actual experimental conditions.

In the superordinate classification task, the participants were presented with the same real objects as were presented in the object decision with regular drawings tasks and had to classify them according to whether they were natural or artefactual.
The viewing conditions and mode of presentation, including 16 practice trials, were the same as for the object decision tasks.
In all tasks the order of the stimuli was randomized.

As previous studies have reported that speed-accuracy tradeoffs are often exhibited by autistic participants (they typically prioritize accuracy over RT) (Van der Hallen et al., 2015), we combined RT (median correct) and accuracy for each participant into a single dependent measure by means of the Balanced Integration Score (BIS) (Liesefeld et al., 2015; Liesefeld & Janczyk, 2019).

text.text: BIS are calculated by standardizing the RT and proportion correct (PC) for each participant and subtracting the standardized RT value (ZRT) from the standardized PC value (ZPC) yielding a BIS for each participant.
Positive BIS indicate performance above the mean of the whole sample (autistic and non-autistic participants) and negative BIS performance below the mean of the whole sample.
As per the preregistration the following analyses were performed.

Simple group differences were examined by means of unpaired t-tests based on bias corrected accelerated bootstrap analyses [1000 samples] (H1) and an unpaired samples t-test based on Bayesian inference (H2).

As H1 was directional, the effect was considered significant if the lower bound of the (two-tailed) bootstrapped 90%CI of the statistical test was positive (BIS are assumed to be higher for non-autistic than for autistic individuals).

Interactions and main effects for H3 were examined by means of a mixed factorial ANOVA with Group (autistic vs non-autistic individuals) as the between-subject factor, and Stimulus Type (regular drawings vs fragmented drawings) and Structural similarity (SS vs SD objects) as within-subject factors.
Because the predictions are directional, effects in the ANOVA will be considered significant if the onetailed p-value is < .05.

text.text: As will become apparent below one non-autistic participant (ID = 219) was an extreme outlier on all object recognition tasks (including the superordinate classification tasks).
This was due to abnormally long RTs with accuracy within the normal range.
It was not the case, however, that the person was impaired on all tasks requiring visual processing.
The person performed quite well (within Object recognition in autism 16 normal range RT) in an embedded figure tasks and in Navon's paradigm.
Hence, the person cannot be excluded on grounds of being inattentive or showing poor compliance.
It is more likely that this person may suffer from a visual object recognition disorder; a possibility we cannot examine further.

4 Discussion It has been proposed that autistic individuals exhibit an altered visual perceptual processing style in that they weigh local shape information more than global shape information (the overall layout of a scene or an object) when they process visual stimuli (Happé & Frith, 2006; Mottron et al., 2006).

text.text: This altered processing style has also been linked to impaired face recognition (Behrmann, Avidan et al., 2006; Behrmann, Thomas et al., 2006) which is often observed in autistic individuals (Griffin et al., 2021; Kamensek et al., 2023; Minio-Paluello et al., 2020).

text.text: Comparatively fewer studies have examined whether object recognition is also affected in autistic individuals -which has been considered likely (Behrmann, Thomas et al., 2006) -and the findings from these studies seem rather inconsistent as discussed in the Introduction.

text.text: In the present study we thus examined visual object recognition in autism in detail by examining performance across three quite demanding visual object recognition tasks, that differed in whether the stimuli presented were regular drawings, silhouettes or fragmented forms.
In addition, we also examined effects of perceptual differentiation and the structural similarity of the objects to be recognized.

Based on the PACE model of visual object processing (Gerlach, 2009 (Gerlach, , 2017b) ) we derived four predictions regarding how autistic individuals -provided that they have a local shape processing bias -should perform relative to non-autistic individuals across a range of tasks where we manipulated degree of structural similarity, stimulus characteristics (salience of global/local information), and task demands (degree of perceptual differentiation required).
text.formatted: Based on the PACE model of visual object processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gerlach, 2009</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Gerlach, , 2017b) )</ref> we derived four predictions regarding how autistic individuals -provided that they have a local shape processing bias -should perform relative to non-autistic individuals across a range of tasks where we manipulated degree of structural similarity, stimulus characteristics (salience of global/local information), and task demands (degree of perceptual differentiation required).

text.text: Our main predictions regarding visual object recognition were that autistic individuals would perform like nonautistic individuals when local shape information is less salient than global shape information and these types of information need not be integrated to any great degree (recognition of silhouettes) [H2], but less efficiently when both types of information are available but global shape information is more important and the demand on shape configuration (the binding of visual elements into elaborate shape descriptions) increases (processing of fragmented forms) [H1/H3].
Finally, we predicted that structurally similar objects would be less efficiently processed by autistic individuals [H3/H4].
The results are easily summarized.
Our second hypothesis, regarding processing of silhouettes, found support.
This suggests that participants in our autism sample can and do process the global shape of objects when this is salient and use of details is limited.
This finding is also what should be expected based on the WCC and EPF accounts.

More surprisingly, the autistic individuals also performed in the range of the non-autistic participants on all other tasks, that is, regardless of whether: (i) the stimuli were fragmented or not, (ii) the demand placed on shape configuration was high or low, or (iii) whether the stimuli were structurally similar or not.
Accordingly, H1, H3, and H4 were not supported.
These findings, however, can also be accounted for by both the WCC and the EPF.

On these accounts, problems with global shape processing should only arise for autistic individuals with a local processing style and maybe such individuals were underrepresented in the present sample.

While we cannot dismiss this possibility, our findings suggest that impaired processing of global shape and/or impaired integration of local and global shape information in the context of visual object recognition is not a general characteristic of individuals with autism.
The present findings add to the variability reported in previous studies of visual object recognition in autism (see table 1).

text.text: Of the 10 studies that reported impaired processing of objects in autism, six examined adult populations of autistic individuals with normal to high intellectual functioning (Ameli et al., 1988; Behrmann, Avidan et al., 2006; Burnett et al., 2015; Loth et al., 2010; O'Hearn et al., 2014; Peristeri et al., 2023) like we did.

text.text: Hence, differences in age and IQ are not likely explanations for the difference in findings.
The same goes for stimulus degradation.
Four of the studies reporting reduced performance in autism used degraded stimulus material (Booth & Happé, 2018; Burnett et al., 2015; Dehaqani et al., 2016; Evers et al., 2014).

text.text: But again, so did we in two of the conditions without seeing any evidence of impairment in the autistic group.
This leaves us with two explanatory possibilities: (i) differences in gender, and (ii) differences in the type of task used.
Regarding option 1, our sample is special in that it comprises a majority of female participants (73%).
In comparison, most other studies are based on male participants only or a majority of males (see table 1).
text.formatted: In comparison, most other studies are based on male participants only or a majority of males (see table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: However, as we are unaware of any systematic gender differences in visual object recognition -as revealed by for example meta-analytical studies -option 1 seems an unlikely explanation.
This leaves us with differences in task type.

Six out of the 10 studies that found impaired object processing in autism used object naming tasks (Booth & Happé, 2018; Burnett et al., 2015; Dehaqani et al., 2016; Evers et al., 2014; Loth et al., 2010; Peristeri et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Six out of the 10 studies that found impaired object processing in autism used object naming tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Booth & Happé, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Burnett et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Dehaqani et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Evers et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Loth et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Peristeri et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In comparison we used object decision tasks, which do not require lexico-semantic processing (Gerlach, 2009 (Gerlach, , 2017b)), and a superordinate classification task that does require access to lexico-semantic knowledge but does not require much lexicon-semantic differentiation as object individuation is not required (Gerlach et al., 2000).
text.formatted: In comparison we used object decision tasks, which do not require lexico-semantic processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gerlach, 2009</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Gerlach, , 2017b))</ref>, and a superordinate classification task that does require access to lexico-semantic knowledge but does not require much lexicon-semantic differentiation as object individuation is not required <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Gerlach et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: This raises the possibility that the reduced performance for autistic individuals on object naming tasks might not necessarily reflect a perceptual but rather a lexico-semantic processing difference between the groups.
This would be interesting to examine more directly in future studies.

It should be noted, however, that not all studies using object naming tasks have found behavioral differences (Caplette et al., 2016; Purpura et al., 2024) so it is unlikely to be the sole explanation for the inconsistency.
text.formatted: It should be noted, however, that not all studies using object naming tasks have found behavioral differences <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Caplette et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Purpura et al., 2024)</ref> so it is unlikely to be the sole explanation for the inconsistency.

text.text: In summary, the present study found no evidence for a behavioral difference in visual object recognition between autistic and non-autistic participants despite using quite demanding tasks.
Examination of previous studies suggests that lower performance for visual object processing in autism is most pronounced on object naming tasks (using degraded stimuli).
This could imply that the difference observed is more lexico-semantic than perceptual in nature, but the picture is far from clear.

A potential limitation of the present study -which also applies to other studies examining visual object recognition in autism -is that the sample was not selected to only include individuals with a local processing style.
It just may be that it is only such individuals who would exhibit impaired performance in tasks that critically depend on processing of global shape information.
